title: Best Dehumidifier for Centipedes (2026): Dry Out Their Hideouts
dek: House centipedes go where it's damp and the bugs they eat are plentiful. Dry the basement and bathroom, seal the gaps, and they lose both reasons to stay.
description: The best dehumidifier for centipedes in basements, crawl spaces and bathrooms — plus the sealing steps that keep house centipedes from coming back.
intro: If you've ever flipped on a basement light and watched a house centipede race up the wall on its fifteen pairs of legs, you already know where they like to live: damp, dark corners. That's why so many people go looking for a **dehumidifier for centipedes**. The logic is sound. House centipedes dry out quickly in low humidity, so they gather in basements, crawl spaces, bathrooms and under sinks, where moisture keeps them alive and where the silverfish, spiders and roaches they hunt also thrive.

Here's the honest part: a dehumidifier is not an exterminator. It won't kill the centipedes you already have, and it won't stop one from wandering in through a gap under the door. What it does do — and does well — is make your basement and bathrooms far less hospitable, so fewer centipedes (and fewer of the insects they eat) settle in. Pair it with a few sealing and cleanup steps and most homes see a real difference within a season.
Below are the dehumidifiers we'd put in each centipede hot spot, chosen for continuous drainage, humidistat accuracy and the right size for the space.

blocks.text: House centipedes lose water through their bodies easily, which is why they cling to damp spaces. Holding a basement at 45–50% doesn't poison them; it just makes the space a poor place to live. It also dries out the mold and damp debris that feed silverfish, springtails and other insects, cutting the centipedes' food supply at the same time.

sections.heading: How we pick dehumidifiers for centipedes

blocks.text: We don't lab-test dehumidifiers. We compare capacity ratings under the 2019 DOE procedure (or AHAM ratings for crawl-space units), ENERGY STAR listings and manufacturer manuals for drainage, operating temperature and controls. Then we read owner reviews for recurring problems — pumps that fail, buckets that crack, sensors that drift — and check CPSC recall records.

For this guide, we weighted **continuous drainage** most heavily, because pest control is a months-long job, not an overnight one. We also matched each pick to the places house centipedes actually live: unfinished basements, crawl spaces and bathrooms.

sections.heading: What to look for in a dehumidifier for centipedes

items.label: Continuous drainage
items.text: A pump or gravity hose lets the unit run for weeks. A bucket that fills and shuts the unit off overnight lets humidity bounce right back.

items.label: Size for the source
items.text: A centipede in the kitchen often started in the basement. Size the dehumidifier for the damp space below, not the room where you spotted it. Our [dehumidifier size guide](/guides/dehumidifier-size-guide/) helps.

items.label: A humidistat you can set
items.text: Pick a model that holds a percentage, then aim for 45–50%. Our [humidistat settings guide](/guides/dehumidifier-humidistat-settings-guide/) covers seasonal targets.

items.label: Low-temperature operation
items.text: Basements and crawl spaces run cool. Look for auto-defrost, or a crawl-space unit rated for temperatures in the 30s or 40s.

items.label: A separate hygrometer
items.text: Check the far corners, not just the air next to the machine.

sections.heading: Will a dehumidifier get rid of centipedes?

blocks.text: On its own, rarely completely — but it's one of the most effective long-term steps you can take. Think of it as removing the two things that keep centipedes indoors: moisture and prey. Once a basement stays dry, the population usually shrinks over a few months because fewer centipedes survive and fewer insects are around to feed them.

What a dehumidifier won't do is stop new arrivals. House centipedes also come in from outdoor mulch, leaf litter and stone piles, slipping under doors and through foundation gaps. That's why the sealing steps below matter as much as the machine.

blocks.title: When to call a pro
blocks.text: If you're seeing centipedes daily, the real issue may be a large population of the insects they eat. A licensed pest control professional can identify what's feeding them and treat that directly.

sections.heading: Pest-proofing steps to pair with your dehumidifier

items: **Fix the water first.** Repair dripping pipes, sweating cold-water lines and leaky washing-machine hoses. Clean gutters and make sure downspouts discharge well away from the foundation.
**Seal entry points.** Caulk gaps around basement windows, utility penetrations and sill plates. Add door sweeps to exterior and basement doors.
**Pull mulch and debris back.** Keep mulch, firewood, leaf piles and stones at least a foot or two from the foundation.
**Declutter the basement.** Cardboard boxes on the floor hold moisture and give insects cover. Switch to sealed plastic bins on shelves.
**Run the bathroom fan.** Leave the exhaust fan on during and for about 20 minutes after showers, and wipe standing water off tub ledges.
**Cover the sump and floor drains.** A tight sump lid and a working trap in floor drains block a common damp hiding spot.
**Use sticky traps to monitor.** Glue traps along basement walls show whether numbers are dropping over time.

The best dehumidifier for centipedes is one that keeps their favorite hideout below 50% humidity, month after month. For most basements that's the **Frigidaire FFAP5033W1** with its built-in pump. Choose the **AlorAir Sentinel HD55** if the problem starts in a crawl space, the **Midea Cube 20** for a bathroom or laundry room, and the **Honeywell TP50AWKN** if a floor drain makes a pump unnecessary. Add a hygrometer, seal the gaps, clear the clutter — and give it a season to work.

faqs.q: Does a dehumidifier get rid of centipedes?
faqs.a: It helps a lot, but it isn't an extermination method. House centipedes need moisture to survive, so keeping a basement or bathroom at 45–50% humidity makes it inhospitable and reduces the insects they eat. Combine it with sealing gaps, fixing leaks and clearing clutter for the best results.

faqs.q: What humidity level keeps centipedes away?
faqs.a: Aim for 45–50% relative humidity in basements and bathrooms. The EPA recommends keeping indoor humidity below 60%, ideally 30–50%, and that same range discourages centipedes, silverfish and mold.

faqs.q: What size dehumidifier do I need for centipedes in my basement?
faqs.a: Most damp basements need a 50-pint unit. Choose one with a built-in pump or put it near a floor drain so it can run continuously. A small, closed-off finished room can get by with 20–35 pints.

faqs.q: Why do I have so many centipedes in my house?
faqs.a: Usually because you have damp areas and plenty of insects for them to eat. Leaks, high basement humidity, mulch against the foundation and cardboard clutter all contribute. Fix the moisture and the food supply and their numbers drop.

faqs.q: How long does it take a dehumidifier to reduce centipedes?
faqs.a: Expect to see a difference over several weeks to a few months. The dehumidifier can dry the air in days, but the population declines gradually as fewer centipedes and prey insects survive in the drier space.
They're mostly a nuisance. House centipedes can bite if handled, which may feel like a minor bee sting, but they don't damage the house or spread disease, and they actually eat other household pests.
